*** This is a major event that reached the UTLS (upper troposphere and lower stratosphere). *** There were around nine pyroCb pulses between 18:30 UTC and 23:25 UTC. Coldest BT is colder than coldest temperature on sounding (-64.1 °C) so the top is at least 13200 m.  The EarthCARE satellite detected layers of aerosols from this event at altitudes up to 13 km just west of James Bay at 06:50 UTC, May 14, east of James Bay at 19:30 UTC, May 14 and up to 14 km (dusty smoke) at 05:57 UTC, May 15 over 51.5 N, 69.0 W. Produced a warm split window BTD signal that was still detectable at 08 UTC, May 15 over the Gulf of St-Lawrence. The aerosols travelled over the Atlantic Ocean and were detected by the Santa Cruz, Tenerife LIDAR (28.47 N, 16.25 W) starting 22:30 UTC, May 16 at an altitude of 9 km. The aerosols gradually extended vertically in time on May 17 to layers with an altitude ranging from 6 km to 13 km (see https://mplnet.gsfc.nasa.gov/data?all&s=Santa_Cruz_Tenerife&t=20250517). The aerosols were also detected by the El Anerosillo LIDAR (37.1 N, 6.7 W) in southern Spain at and altitude of 14 km at 00 UTC, May 18 (see https://mplnet.gsfc.nasa.gov/data?all&s=El_Arenosillo&t=20250518). Backtrajectories point to in time and space to this blowup in Manitoba.  On May 19, OMPS-LP on Suomi NPP (10:57 UTC) and N21 (11:23 UTC) detected the smoke aerosols over Bulgaria at an altitude up to 14.5 km. This is two to three km above the tropopause. On May 20, 09:42 UTC, EarthCARE detected the aerosols over Kazakhstan at altitudes of 9 to 13 km.

The closest rawinsonde station, The Pas, Canada, could not be used to determine the maximum injection height because of the many possible values resulting from the vertical temperature profile. Luckily, EarthCARE passed directly over the plume of this pyroCb at 08:03 UTC and detected aerosols at an altitude of 9000 m at 53.2 N, 101.0 W. Suomi NPP at 08:43 UT detected a coldest BT of -47 °C at that location. As a result, the maximum injection altitude is at least 9000 m. Max AI and coordinates determined by tracking split-window BTD and IR. Much higher values produced by the many fires in the region over the past days were detected over Ontario and Hudson Bay. See https://cimss.ssec.wisc.edu/satellite-blog/archives/65147.
